summary.text: The Galactic Center is the barycenter of the Milky Way, with a supermassive black hole of about 4 million solar masses called Sagittarius A* at its middle.
It lies about 26,000 light-years from Earth toward Sagittarius, Ophiuchus and Scorpius, where the Milky Way appears brightest.
Interstellar dust hides it at visible and ultraviolet wavelengths, so astronomers learn about it from gamma ray, hard X-ray, infrared, submillimetre and radio observations.

facts.label: Central object
facts.value: Black hole of about 4 million solar masses

facts.label: Stars near center
facts.value: About 10 million within one parsec, mostly red giants

facts.label: Clear viewing gap
facts.value: Baade's Window, a one-degree-wide void in the dust lanes

facts.label: Coordinate zero point
facts.value: Sagittarius A, adopted by the IAU in 1958

items.prompt: An astronomer points an ordinary optical telescope at the middle of our galaxy and sees almost nothing of it. Why?

options.label: The black hole there absorbs all light headed for Earth
Dust along the line of sight blocks visible light
It is too distant for any telescope to detect
It gives off no light of any kind

items.explain: Interstellar dust along the line of sight stops us studying it at visible, ultraviolet or soft X-ray wavelengths.

items.prompt: In the early 1940s, Walter Baade searched near the star Alnasl for a way to look toward the galaxy's core in visible light. What did he find?

options.label: A narrow void in the dust lanes with a clear view of stars
A giant bright star that outshone the whole core
A ring of gas that glowed in visible light
A second black hole orbiting the first

items.explain: He found a one-degree-wide void in the interstellar dust lanes, now called Baade's Window.

items.prompt: In 1954 radio astronomers found an intense point-source near the middle of a belt of radio emission in Sagittarius, about 32 degrees from where astronomers then supposed the middle to be. What did they conclude?

options.label: The source was a nearby star unrelated to the Galaxy's middle
The source sat at the true center, so the older guess was off
The source was too far from the old guess to matter
The source was just a bright patch of dust

items.explain: They named it Sagittarius A and realised it was at the very center of the Galaxy.

items.prompt: In 2008, telescopes linked across Hawaii, Arizona and California measured the radio source at the galaxy's core as 44 million kilometres wide. How does that compare with distances in our own Solar System?

options.label: Wider than Earth's whole distance from the Sun
About as wide as Earth's orbit around the Sun
Barely larger than the Sun itself
Slightly less than Mercury's closest distance to the Sun

items.explain: Mercury is 46 million kilometres from the Sun at its closest, so the radio source is slightly narrower than that distance.

items.prompt: If you could count stars in the tiny space right around the black hole at the galaxy's heart, what would you find?

options.label: Millions of stars, mostly old red giants, with many massive ones too
A few dozen young blue stars and little else
Almost empty space with a handful of dim stars
Mostly small dwarf stars, with no massive ones

items.explain: About 10 million stars sit in the central cubic parsec, most of them old red giants, and the region is also rich in massive stars.

items.prompt: A radio source at the core is much larger than the object at the very center. What is thought to power it?

options.label: Starlight bouncing off the dust that surrounds the center
Gas falling toward the black hole, probably through a disk, releasing energy
The black hole's own heat, slowly leaking out
Radio waves left behind by the early universe

items.explain: Accretion of gas onto the black hole, probably involving an accretion disk, would release energy to power the radio source.
